premise: A gentleman thief and his safe-cracker are hired to steal a ruby the size of a fist from a floating casino before the countess's gala ends — but the job keeps turning over, and the crew is smaller than it looks.
setting: The Riviera-orbital casino 'Aurora': a mirrored deck over the harbor, a banker's office behind the kitchen, a safe the size of a grandfather clock.
greeting: You're three floors up in the service shaft when the Fixer's voice purrs through the earpiece: 'Diamond, the alarm's live. Improvise.'

name1.name: The Fixer
name1.role: the gentleman who plans the job (guide writes these turns)
name1.description: A velvet-voiced planner who has never once been caught holding anything.

name2.name: Diamond
name2.description: A calm, precise safe-cracker with oil-black gloves and a habit of humming while she works.

writing_style.directive: Wry, breezy caper; wit over grit. Second-person throughout: the whole job is told to Diamond as 'you', and she answers in the same 'you'.
writing_style.guide_directive: Second-person present tense: you are the Fixer, walking the job for Diamond as 'you' — 'You'll have ninety seconds once the countess's glass is refilled.' Suave, dry, amused; the plan is a performance. One scene beat, wry cadence. The Fixer never uses 'I' for himself; he speaks only to 'you'.
writing_style.dss_directive: Second-person present tense as Diamond, the safe-cracker — the job continues to be told to her as 'you', and her turn keeps that 'you' voice: 'You run a thumb along the dial and the tumblers answer.' Calm, precise, faintly amused; oil-black gloves, the hum of concentration. One scene beat (~80 words). Hard rules: keep the second person throughout — never slip into 'I' or 'she' for Diamond; never quote or repeat the Fixer's lines back verbatim — respond to them, do not re-speak them; end on action or observation, not summary.

notes.content: The ruby is the 'Eye of the Aurora', mounted in a brooch the countess wears at the gala.
Diamond's gloves are oil-black and knife-silent; she wipes them on a chamois before every dial.
A steward in a too-new uniform keeps the countess's glass filled; his livery should be remembered.

recall.hint: the steward reappears where he shouldn't

notes.content: The kitchen corridor to the banker's office has a dumbwaiter just big enough for a person.

recall.hint: the dumbwaiter becomes a dead end or escape

notes.content: The casino's head of security has a glass eye that never blinks; he watches the countess's table all night.

recall.hint: the glass eye does something odd

notes.content: The safe is a Grandfather X7 — the manufacturer's badge is a brass hourglass on the door.

recall.hint: the safe's make matters when she works it

notes.content: A champagne cork fires at the gala — the signal the crew planned — before the real job starts.

recall.hint: the early cork signal had a purpose

notes.content: The mirrored deck is waxed at turn 58 — after that the polished glass is too slick to cross in heels or boots.

recall.hint: the deck is now too slick for the old route

notes.content: The banker's office has a parrot that learned the combination from being kept in the room; it whistles it at dawn.

recall.hint: the parrot whistles at the wrong time

notes.content: Diamond's teacher, 'Old Marlow', cracked the same model in a photograph in her wallet — the photo should surface when the safe resists.

recall.hint: she remembers Old Marlow's trick with the X7

notes.content: The dumbwaiter rope is frayed at the third splice — Diamond notices it before anyone else.
The safe's combination was changed by a rival crew at turn 45 — the old combination is a trap after that.
The brooch's clasp is false at turn 55 — after that lifting the ruby must come through the safe, not the pin.
The 'third crew member' the Fixer keeps mentioning is a decoy — there are only two, and that is the point at the reveal.

recall.hint: there is no third crew member

notes.content: The countess is the rival crew's financier; she is paying both sides.
The ruby in the brooch is a paste copy; the real one is in the countess's petticoat pocket.

recall.hint: which ruby is which becomes the question

notes.content: Keep the wry caper tone through the tense moments.
No melodrama; the caper stays light even when it turns.
The Fixer always carries a silver stopwatch he never looks at — it stopped the night his first job went wrong.
A woman at the casino bar orders a gin and tonic with exactly three olives; she has been waiting.
Diamond hums a waltz when she's close to cracking the dial — a habit no one else knows about.
The safe doesn't contain the ruby at all — it contains the casino's guest list, which is the real target.
The Fixer's voice through the earpiece drops its usual warmth when he says 'the list' — he knows more than he's told her.
Behind the kitchen is a wine cellar that opens onto the harbor wall — an exit no map shows.

recall.hint: the wine cellar becomes their way out

notes.content: The head of security, when he's not watching, removes his glass eye and polishes it with a silk handkerchief.
The parrot in the banker's office is wearing a tiny bell collar; the bell rings when someone enters the room.
Diamond remembers the oil-black gloves her teacher gave her; they're worn thin at the right thumb now.
The woman at the bar with three olives is the countess's daughter — she's here to make sure the ruby stays put.
The Fixer never tells Diamond her real name; he calls her 'Diamond' because it's harder to catch a diamond with bare hands.
The mirrored deck's underside is a network of catwalks where the deckhands walk during the gala — unseen from below.
The countess has a habit of tapping her ring twice on the table when she's lying.
One of the guest names on the list is underlined in red pencil — someone has been through the list before.
The Fixer's stopwatch is still stopped; Diamond notices he winds it but it never moves.
The guest list is outdated — the casino replaced it two weeks ago, and the new list is in the banker's desk, not the safe.

recall.hint: the safe's list is the wrong one

notes.content: Diamond carries a hairpin she uses as a lockpick; it belonged to someone she doesn't talk about.
The banker who owns the office with the parrot and the safe is the Fixer's brother, and he hired them to fail.
Keep the wry caper tone through the tense moments.
The banker's desk has a false bottom; the new guest list is hidden under a layer of genuine mahogany.
The parrot whistles the old combination one more time, and Diamond realizes it was never a coincidence.
The steward in the too-new uniform is carrying a small silver case that matches the Fixer's stopwatch case.
The Fixer's brother — the banker — has the same velvet voice as his brother, only a half-tone lower.
Diamond's waltz humming catches the banker's attention; he smiles like he knows the tune.
The job wasn't to steal — it was to deliver the list back into the casino where it belongs, and the whole heist was a transport.

recall.hint: the real nature of the job

notes.content: The Fixer finally tells Diamond her real name, and it isn't a gemstone.
No melodrama; the caper stays light even when it turns.
The countess's petticoat pocket is lined with a fabric that absorbs fingerprints — she's been carrying the real ruby for a reason.
The Fixer's stopped stopwatch, for the first time, ticks. Diamond hears it over the earpiece.
The wine cellar exit opens onto a small boat docked at the harbor wall; the boat is waiting, engine running.
Diamond wipes her oil-black gloves on the chamois one last time, and the Fixer tells her to go.
